title: What CoFlow does
description: CoFlow keeps your team’s engineering standards in one reviewed place, gives them to coding agents for each task and checks the result.
text: In one paragraph CoFlow holds the rules your team expects code to follow, the facts agents keep needing about your system, and the lessons your team learns from reviews, corrections and incidents. It gives coding agents the rules that apply to the files they are about to change, reviews pull requests against the same rules, and runs review agents whose actions people approve. People decide what becomes a rule. No agent can merge, approve a pull request, push or bypass a check. How the pieces fit Start from the starter rule packs that match your stack. coflow init picks them from your manifests. Connect your coding agents. They read the rules through their own rule files and the CoFlow MCP server. Review changes. coflow check runs locally; the hosted service reviews pull requests. Capture what goes wrong: review findings, corrections in agent sessions, reverts, tickets and production incidents. The lessons pipeline turns repeated evidence into rule proposals. A person reviews each one; a pull request makes it active. Watch the scorecard, the cost ledger and the evaluation runs to see whether the rules help. Where to go next Quickstart Install the CLI, initialize a repository and connect a coding agent. Starter library What the starter packs cover and how your own rules take over. Review and tool checks What runs locally, what runs on the hosted worker and what “not run” means. Agent Studio Seventeen agent templates, the autonomy ladder and approvals. Security Tenant isolation, roles, approvals and agent limits. Plans and billing The planned launch plans, trial and credits. Availability CoFlow is in private build. These guides describe the pilot release. Some features work only after an operator configures them, and some are not ready yet. The feature status page lists which is which. Publishing documentation does not turn on a feature in your workspace. Ask about the pilot .

title: Quickstart
description: Put your team’s standards in front of a coding agent, check a change and see a rule proposal, on your own repository.
text: Install the CLI The local workflow needs no account, no server and no model key. CoFlow is a Python package with a coflow command. Install it into its own virtual environment from the source your onboarding contact gives you, then check that the command works: python3 -m venv ~/coflow-env ~/coflow-env/bin/pip install <package source from onboarding> export PATH="$HOME/coflow-env/bin:$PATH" coflow --help coflow --help lists init , validate , scan , compile , export , check , inbox and the other commands. The commands are written for macOS and Linux. Initialize a repository cd ~/src/your-repo coflow init coflow validate coflow compile --paths app/main.py init reads your manifests (for example pyproject.toml , package.json or alembic.ini ), prints the packs it chose, copies them to .coflow/rules/ , writes .coflow/config.yaml and generates AGENTS.md , the Copilot instructions, the Cursor rules and the agent skills. Choose packs yourself with --packs , or a named set with --bundle . compile prints the rules an agent gets for that path, cut to the token budget. Commit .coflow/ and the generated files so the whole team gets them. Connect your coding agent coflow connect claude --dry-run coflow connect claude Name your client: claude , cursor , vscode (GitHub Copilot), codex , gemini , windsurf , cline , zed , jetbrains , amazonq , roo or aider . coflow connect --all connects every client whose own files are already in the repository. --dry-run prints the diff of each file first. connect writes the client’s rule files and merges a coflow server into the client’s project MCP file, keeping every other server there. Windsurf, Cline and Zed keep MCP servers in a user-level file, so for them it prints the entry to paste. Aider has no MCP client and gets rule files only. The local MCP server needs no token. To use the hosted service instead, add --hosted ; the client then reads your credential from the COFLOW_API_TOKEN environment variable, which you set in your shell. connect never writes a token into a file. See coding agents and MCP server and CLI . What the agent gets The local server offers fifteen tools: five rule tools, eight context tools, get_budget and record_cost . The ones to start with: get_standards : the rules for the files of the task, ordered and cut to a token budget. get_rule : the full text of one rule, with its examples. record_outcome : the agent reports whether it followed a rule. propose_rule : the agent proposes a rule. It lands in .coflow/proposals/ and does nothing until a person merges it. where_is and remember : facts about your system the agent looked up once. Tell the agent once: “Before you change code, call get_standards for the files you will touch.” Check a change git diff | coflow check --diff - Exit code 0 means clean and 1 means a required rule is broken. With --strict , exit code 2 means a rule in scope had no check run. A rule enforced by a tool that is not installed is reported as not run, never as passed. Rules that need a model review are listed as “not reviewed (no model)” until you configure a model. See a rule proposal Correct the agent in a session, for example “always pass a timeout to requests calls”. When it agrees the correction is a standing rule, it calls propose_rule and a file appears in .coflow/proposals/ . You can also capture corrections: coflow connect claude --capture (or cursor , gemini ) installs the client’s end-of-session hook. For other clients, record one yourself with coflow lesson "always pass a timeout to requests calls" . coflow inbox lists what was captured. A proposal is never active. A person reviews it and merges the rule file in a pull request. Run coflow export after that so the agent files carry the new rule. Next steps coflow scan shows the detected tools and the packs it proposes. coflow context setup writes five questions about your system for a person to answer once. The hosted service adds pull request review, the approvals inbox, Agent Studio and chat approvals. See Connect and Agent Studio .

title: Feature status
description: What ships in the pilot release, what works once an operator configures it, and what is not ready.
text: Shipped in the pilot release This code is on the pilot release branch and runs without extra provider setup: The coflow CLI and the local MCP server: init , scan , compile , export , check , connect for 12 coding agents, lesson , inbox , context , search , eval , cost , evidence-pack and the others. The starter rule packs, starter bundles, stack detection and the generated agent files. Local review with 13 linter and scanner adapters (each runs when it is installed) and host checks. The lessons pipeline, rule proposals and approval policies with reviewer groups. The hosted API, the approvals inbox, and Agent Studio with 17 agent templates seeded at shadow. Organization-owned CoFlow tables under forced row-level security. The scorecard, the cost ledger, the evaluation datasets and harness, and the compliance evidence pack. Works once configured These are in the release but do nothing until an operator sets them up for your organization: Pull request review on GitHub: needs the GitHub App or the Nango connection. An operator must confirm a GitHub App installation before it routes anything. GitLab and Bitbucket Cloud review: each host is turned on separately. The hosted MCP service: off by default, and requires agent credentials. Agent Studio runs on real pull requests: start once your organization binds an agent to a repository. Model-backed review: rules that need a model stay “not reviewed (no model)” until a model is configured. Slack and Microsoft Teams approvals: need the chat app installed for your workspace. Production evidence from Datadog, Sentry, PagerDuty, Opsgenie and CloudWatch: needs a source configuration with credential references. Scheduled work (weekly scorecard, nightly host snapshots, approval escalation and expiry, ops ingest, agent schedules): nothing runs on a schedule until an operator creates the jobs. See scheduled jobs . Not ready yet Do not plan a pilot around these: Opening a ticket from an agent: no Jira or Linear connection for agent tickets ships yet. An approved ticket action fails with a note that says so, and nothing is sent. Proposal pull requests: an agent’s proposal pull request adds one file under .coflow/proposals/ , is always a draft and never changes rules. Approving on the Proposals screen returns the rule file text and does not open a pull request. Agent Studio runs on GitLab and Bitbucket: studio agent runs are GitHub only in this release. The other hosts get the plain review. Tool checks on the hosted worker: the worker image installs ruff, bandit, zizmor, actionlint and hadolint, and runs them only on files it can rebuild whole from the patch (new files, or patches that start at line 1). Every other tool check on the server is reported as not run. See review and tool checks . Hosted MCP: accepts organization-wide agent credentials only; a credential bound to a project is refused. Call budgets are kept per process, so run one instance. Repository access inside an organization: repositories are not tied to workspace projects yet, so any member can read any repository’s CoFlow records in their organization. Some scorecard metrics on a fresh pilot: reviewer agreement needs 20 findings with a disposition, and repeat rate needs evidence linked to a rule. The scorecard says “not measured” with the reason. The server’s detected system map is whatever coflow sync last posted, and the server flags stale facts by age only. Screens not built yet: chat settings, rule sync grants, host snapshots, decision history and evidence on its own. Their routes exist. Live accounts: the GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket integrations were built and tested against recorded fakes, not against live accounts. Treat the first repository on each host as a test. The same applies to the other vendor integrations; see Connect . Promotion above shadow: the proposed precision and recall thresholds have not been validated against a hosted model or real pull requests. Billing: the plans, trial and credits on plans and billing are the planned launch model and are not live. Confirm your workspace Ask during onboarding for the deployed version, the integrations configured for your organization, your sign-in URL and your role. Use your workspace and its release evidence, not the examples on this website, to decide what is live.

title: Plans, trial and billing
description: Two plans priced per developer seat, a 14-day trial and monthly credits for model and compute-heavy work.
text: Status Planned launch billing model. This page describes the billing model being built for launch. It is not live: CoFlow is in private build, nothing on this website takes payment, and the values below are proposed starting values that may change before launch. Two plans CoFlow is priced per developer seat, billed monthly or annually. There are two plans: Plan Seat price Included credits What it adds Team To be confirmed 1,000 per seat per month Starter rule packs and your own rules, compiled context, the MCP server and CLI, review, the lessons pipeline, Agent Studio and approvals Business To be confirmed 3,000 per seat per month Everything in Team, plus single sign-on (SSO) and SOC 2 Type II audit support Seat prices and the discount for annual billing are to be confirmed. Prices will be in US dollars and exclude tax. 14-day free trial The trial lasts 14 days and includes 2,000 credits for the organization. A payment card is required to start the trial. At the end of the trial it converts to a paid subscription on the plan you chose, unless you cancel before then. Business security Business includes single sign-on and SOC 2 Type II audit support. Single sign-on needs identity configuration for your organization. Audit support covers readiness and evidence workflows, such as the compliance evidence pack . These docs do not assert that CoFlow holds an issued SOC 2 Type II report. Read organizations, roles and approvals and RLS and tenant isolation . Credits in brief Credits pay for model and compute-heavy work: evaluations, lesson drafting and testing, agent sandbox, shadow and live runs, and model-backed review. Rules, compiled context, the MCP server, host checks and linters never use credits. Monthly credits do not roll over. Credit packs add more. Details are on credits and usage . During the private build Pilot terms are agreed with each team directly. The website prepares an enquiry email; it does not sell plans, start trials or take card details. Talk to us about the pilot .

title: Credits and usage
description: What credits pay for, what never uses them, credit packs and how usage is shown.
text: Status Planned launch billing model. This page describes the billing model being built for launch. It is not live: CoFlow is in private build, nothing on this website takes payment, and the values below are proposed starting values that may change before launch. What credits pay for Evaluations: harness and dataset runs that call a model. Lessons: drafting rule proposals from evidence and testing them. Agent runs: sandbox, shadow and live runs in Agent Studio. Model-backed review: review steps that need a model. What never uses credits Deterministic features never use credits and keep working when the balance is zero: rules and rule packs, compiled context, the MCP server, host checks, and the linters and scanners CoFlow runs. Monthly allowance Credits Team 1,000 per seat per month Business 3,000 per seat per month Trial 2,000 per organization Monthly credits do not roll over to the next month. Credit packs One credit is worth $0.01. Packs add credits on top of the monthly allowance: Pack Credits $50 5,000 $200 20,000 $1,000 100,000 Pack credits expire 12 months after purchase. Auto top-up is optional. When it is on, it buys a pack when the balance runs low, up to a monthly cap you set. How a run is charged Cost before the run: CoFlow shows what a run will cost and reserves the credits before it starts. Failed runs: credits for a run that fails are refunded. Low balance: when the balance cannot cover a run, the run is refused rather than started and left half done. Seeing your usage A usage meter in the app shows the balance and what has been used this month. The Usage page breaks usage down and exports it as CSV. Credits are separate from the cost ledger , which records the tokens and runner minutes your own coding agents and models use, priced with your own contract prices. Your coding-agent subscriptions are also separate.

title: Rules, lessons and human review
description: Keep guidance scoped, evidence-backed and versioned.
text: Engineering rules registry Rules include applicability, exceptions, priority, evidence and links to versioned skills or evaluations. Applicability can use project, repository, file paths, task type and technology. The effective rule is the latest approved revision; a pending draft does not silently replace it. Review and revisions Proposals enter a review workflow. Authorized reviewers approve, reject or request changes. Corrections create new revisions rather than rewriting approved history. When your workspace signs in with single sign-on, the person who wrote a rule cannot also approve it. A second verified teammate has to sign off. Distillation and improvement proposals CoFlow can group approved observations and propose improvements. The documented distillation path uses deterministic grouping and templates; it is not unrestricted semantic synthesis. The improvement heartbeat analyzes configured project outcomes and creates review candidates. It never approves its own suggestions. Rules for RLS-sensitive application work Capture requirements for tenant identity, authorized project scope, protected writes and pooled connections as project rules. Link positive and negative acceptance checks. CoFlow supplies reviewed guidance; your application, database policies and test runner enforce and verify the behavior. Read the RLS guide .

title: Task-specific instructions
description: Select approved guidance with explicit reasons, dependency pins and budget checks.
text: How selection works Start with the task and explicit file, repository and technology inputs. Applicability categories must match; entries within a category are alternatives. Approved exceptions can exclude a rule. Selection reasons help you inspect why guidance was included or excluded. What a package contains A persisted package can include approved rules, pinned skills, required evaluations, visual references and supporting lessons. Reopen it through GET /v1/instructions/{id} . Historical reads preserve the original package rather than reconstructing it from today’s rules. Token efficiency Budget checks keep optional context bounded. Required guidance is not silently dropped to fit a budget. Instruction-size accounting uses a conservative UTF-8 byte upper bound, not an exact tokenizer measurement. Measure actual model input/output tokens and retries separately when assessing savings. When compilation blocks Declared conflicts, missing approved dependencies or required instructions that exceed the allowed budget can produce a blocked package. Resolve the underlying rule or dependency issue and compile again. Arbitrary contradictions in natural-language rules are not automatically detected.

title: Acceptance checks and outcome metrics
description: Measure what happened without confusing reported outcomes with independent verification.
text: Acceptance contracts Specifications capture requirements, positive/negative checks and source references in immutable revisions. Approval checks the expected revision and digest, with a different recorded principal. Compile an approved specification with a code SHA to bind the acceptance contract into the instruction package. Execution and evidence Required checks run in your development or verification environment. Clients submit pass, fail or skipped results with evidence. Skipped checks do not count as passes. Freshness checks bind current specification/package/code references; they are not evidence that tests were independently executed. Metrics you can inspect Ready and blocked instruction packages, feedback coverage and reported outcomes. Per-revision rule deliveries and reported violations. Retrieval recall and reciprocal rank for approved evaluation sets. Instruction budget estimates, measured separately from provider token usage. Feedback coverage uses ready packages as its denominator. Reported success rates use recorded outcomes and remain empty when none exist. Source windows and bounded datasets must remain visible when interpreting dashboard totals. Measure your pilot Compare similar tasks using the same model and acceptance criteria. Track actual total tokens, review rounds, repeat findings and time to an accepted change. These pilot measurements do not establish a universal savings or compliance percentage. Plan a pilot .

title: Workflow Studio
description: Turn self-contained HTML prototypes into reviewed, editable workflow evidence.
text: Upload and capture Upload self-contained HTML pages and select an entry page. Playback uses an opaque-origin sandbox. Record interactions, form validation, error states and in-bundle navigation. Captures are validated and converted into workflow state graphs. Edit, review and link Relabel and annotate states or transitions, and add clearly marked manual steps. Each save creates an immutable revision. Authorized reviewers approve or reject revisions. Links to requirements and bugs pin the workflow revision, capture and source provenance. Replay and export checks Replay the trace and compare settled states. Export a Playwright test using stable locators where available. Unstable selectors are flagged with suggested test IDs. Unreviewed exports carry a warning; review them before adding them to monitoring. Evidence and isolation Replay results are client-reported, not independent server verification. Uploaded HTML is untrusted and cannot run in the application origin. The sandbox blocks many external interactions, but it is not a fully network-isolated server-side browser. Use synthetic input and avoid entering secrets into prototypes. Workflow records use organization ownership, project authorization and forced PostgreSQL RLS. Read the isolation guide .

title: Row-level security (RLS) and tenant isolation
description: Two separate concerns: protecting CoFlow data and guiding RLS-sensitive application changes.
text: RLS inside CoFlow The PostgreSQL tenant implementation uses forced row-level security on protected tables, with organization ownership and server-resolved project scope. Application authorization checks also apply. Organization isolation alone does not grant access to every project. Verified identity establishes transaction-local app.organization_id and app.authorized_projects . Caller-supplied tenant headers are not an authorization source. Organization context without authorized project scope exposes no project records under the project-aware policies. Runtime requirements Use a restricted application role that does not own protected tables, is not a superuser, and cannot bypass RLS. Backfill existing rows to verified organization/project ownership before activation. Apply reviewed migrations through a separate authorized migration role. Set transaction-local context for API, MCP and worker database operations, including after commits. Verify missing-context denial, cross-tenant read/write denial and pooled-connection reuse against PostgreSQL. SQLite development tests do not prove PostgreSQL RLS behavior. Startup guards check schema and role requirements; behavioral isolation tests remain necessary. RLS in applications built with CoFlow Use CoFlow to give coding agents approved RLS requirements before they change a protected route, migration or background job. Add an acceptance contract that covers both allowed and denied behavior. Example rule: tenant-scoped invoice access Resolve the organization from verified identity. Set its context in the query transaction. Require project authorization. Never treat possession of an invoice ID as permission. This is engineering guidance for your implementation. CoFlow does not install, enable or certify RLS policies in your application merely because a rule is approved. A useful acceptance checklist Tenant A can read and update its own authorized records. Tenant B cannot read, update, insert into or delete Tenant A’s records. Missing organization or project scope fails closed. Connection reuse does not retain another tenant’s context. Workers and evaluations use the same authorization boundaries as API requests. Cache, search and vocabulary results remain tenant and project scoped. Source includes dedicated PostgreSQL RLS tests, including Workflow Studio isolation with a restricted non-bypass role. Confirm the evidence for the exact release deployed to your environment.

title: Organizations, projects and permissions
description: Control access through verified membership, role permissions and project assignments.
text: Membership and sign-in CoFlow signs people in through your identity provider with single sign-on and keeps their access in step with their membership there. Local suspension and project permissions remain authoritative. Organization switching remounts the workspace in the new verified context. Roles and project access Built-in role templates include owner, admin, maintainer, contributor and viewer. Owners can manage organization-specific policies and custom roles. Direct project roles intersect with organization permissions; team assignments cannot elevate the organization role. Archived or deleted projects do not grant access. Approval and audit Knowledge read, capture and review are separate permissions. Sensitive changes append audit records. With single sign-on turned on, authors cannot approve their own knowledge. A second teammate reviews it. Last-owner protections help prevent administrative lockout. Before inviting users Confirm the deployed schema, restricted database role, single sign-on configuration, first owner and project assignments. Test with two organizations, including access revocation and cross-tenant denial. Availability depends on the deployed release and configured identity flow.

title: Coding agents, MCP and source connections
description: Connect reviewed engineering context without assuming every adapter is enabled.
text: Local MCP The checked-in CoFlow MCP server runs over stdio and delegates calls to the authenticated API. Core tools include compile_instructions , record_outcome , get_context , capture_memory and export_workspace . Approval remains a separate authorized API/UI workflow. Use the installed python -m app.mcp_server entry point, your provisioned MEMORY_API_URL and an authorized MEMORY_API_TOKEN supplied through your local secure environment. Never paste credential values into repository configuration. Agent instructions and exports Approved workspace exports return AGENTS.md and MEMORY.md content without writing files on your machine. Review and place the exports in the workspace your agent reads. Local MCP compatibility depends on the client’s ability to launch a stdio server and use your approved configuration. GitHub and Jira The integration implementation includes organization-owned GitHub/Jira connection flows through Nango. GitHub capture uses an allowlisted repository and creates pending knowledge for review. Source-sync jobs require configured queues/workers and recheck authorization. Jira connection authorization does not imply issue synchronization is available. MCP configuration catalog The catalog versions, validates, reviews and audits MCP server descriptors. An approved descriptor starts disabled, and enablement requires a separate reviewed flag. Catalog records do not launch processes, connect to external servers or resolve secrets. Availability limits Do not use a sample hosted MCP URL as proof of a live CoFlow service. The stdio server in source is distinct from a remote HTTP/OAuth connector. Account provisioning, provider adapters and runtime flags must be verified for the release you use.

title: Troubleshooting
description: Start with the boundary that is blocking the workflow.
text: I can sign in but cannot open a project Have an administrator check active local membership, current provider membership, project assignment and project status. Provider login is not enough. Do not work around the issue by adding a tenant ID to a request header. Compilation is blocked Read the blocker and selection reasons. Check approved rule revisions, declared conflict groups, pinned dependency status and required instruction size. Resolve the source issue and compile a new package; historical packages remain immutable. Rows disappear after enabling RLS Confirm ownership backfill and transaction-local organization plus authorized project scope. Use the correct restricted runtime role. Verify PostgreSQL behavior in a disposable environment before rollout; do not disable production policies to make a query return rows. An integration or module is unavailable Check that the exact deployed release contains the feature, its flags are enabled, and the provider/worker configuration is complete. A stored connection or catalog entry alone does not prove an adapter is active. Ask for help Send the module, safe error code, approximate time and deployed version to support@getcoflow.ai . Share package IDs only through an approved support channel. Do not include tokens, personal data or private source content.
